questions.explanation: Fact 5 uses the Danish rescue to separate the physical act from its legal and moral context. A boat can mean different things in different systems.

reviewCards.front: When blame takes over, where does attention land first?
reviewCards.back: It sends attention toward a villain or hero. That feels clear, but it can hide incentives, laws, logistics, institutions, and feedback loops that keep shaping the outcome.

reviewCards.front: How does Peter Senge's systems thinking change a repeated failure?
reviewCards.back: It asks what mechanism keeps producing the failure. The named person may still matter, but the loop, rule, or incentive must be found before the repair can last.

reviewCards.front: Why is UNICEF procurement not a lone-hero story?
reviewCards.back: The low prices depend on tenders, supply chains, standards, and suppliers that can deliver. The achievement is institutional, not just one generous person's gift.

reviewCards.front: What does Dr. Mosoka Fallah's Ebola work make visible beyond hero praise?
reviewCards.back: His Monrovia contact tracing shows local trust, government employees, records, and community knowledge at work. The person matters, and so does the system carrying him.

reviewCards.front: Why can blaming only smugglers miss part of the refugee boat story?
reviewCards.back: Carrier penalties, confiscation risks, smuggling rules, and asylum rights can block safer routes. The smuggler may be guilty while the rules still shape the trap.

reviewCards.front: How would you, in one sentence, connect the single perspective instinct (Ch 8) to the blame-instinct move?
reviewCards.back: The single perspective instinct leans on one favored tool; the blame instinct settles on one face. Both stop the search early, before the system behind the result is in view.

implementationPlan.title: Ask What Made This Possible
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice pausing at the first name your anger or praise wants to choose. Ask What Made This Possible by naming the person, then listing the rule, incentive, route, or routine that made the result likely. The skill keeps responsibility while finding causes that can be changed.

ifThenPlans.context: When the same problem returns with a new person attached
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same failure has a new face, then Ask What Made This Possible by sketching the loop before naming fault.

ifThenPlans.context: When a good result makes one person sound like the whole cause
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise narrows to one hero, then Ask What Made This Possible by naming the tender, route, worker, or routine behind the result.

ifThenPlans.context: When a visible wrongdoer makes the story feel finished
ifThenPlans.plan: If the culprit seems obvious, then Ask What Made This Possible by checking which rules shaped the available choices.

ifThenPlans.context: When someone says system talk lets people off the hook
ifThenPlans.plan: If responsibility gets confused with diagnosis, then Ask What Made This Possible and say which task you are doing first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: When a bad result makes one name jump out, slow down and write a repeatable cause beside it; let that, not the name, decide where responsibility sits.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, put the news app or bookmark you open first inside a folder named "What made this possible?" Watch whether the folder name changes the first cause you name.

memorableLines.text: Blame spends heat before it buys light.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the emotional cost of blaming too soon.

memorableLines.text: A hero can hide the helpers.
memorableLines.why: It makes the praise side of the instinct easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: Responsibility starts after the causes are named.
memorableLines.why: It states the hard edge without excusing people.

chapters.title: The Urgency Instinct
chapters.hook: A dugout canoe slides past the roadblock while the urgent order waits at the gate.
chapters.counterintuition: Urgency is not courage, but pressure with a stopwatch. Real danger needs action, yet the first fast order can miss the route the danger actually uses.
chapters.tryThisNow: When an urgent claim crowds your day, write one rushed miss and the next cleaner check before you forward, approve, or repeat it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Act on real danger, but keep one data check, one side-effect check, and one small next step alive before urgency turns thinking into theater.

breakdown.fastRead:
A dugout canoe moves along the Kwilu River while a roadblock waits on the road. In Nature 2014, David L. Heymann warned that past Ebola controls could look firm and still fail. In Kikwit 1995, contacts under watch could move by canoe or forest path. The urgent order had muscle. The virus had routes.

The urgency instinct is the pull to act now, narrow choices, and stop asking. It is useful when a child is bleeding or a fire is spreading. It is dangerous when a problem has hidden paths, delayed data, or side effects. Panic is speed without a steering wheel.

The useful move is not delay. Use Check the Urgent Route. Ask which route carries the danger, how fresh the data is, and which small step preserves learning. Then act. Speed helps only when it is aimed.
breakdown.deepRead:
Urgency narrows the room before the facts have entered it. A loud deadline makes the mind want two boxes: block or fail, act or deny, believe or ignore. Complex risks rarely fit those boxes. Ebola travels through contacts. Emissions reports travel through slow official systems. Migration numbers travel through source chains that may be thin.

Yvonne has a map open in Kikwit. The road cordon takes most of the ink. Then someone marks the Kwilu River and the forest paths. A visible barrier can hide a leaky route. If she spends every hour proving the checkpoint is strict, she may miss the canoe that keeps moving. The better question is physical: where can a contact still pass?

The same pattern sits inside climate data. A fresh-looking climate graphic can make every related number feel current. In the OECD December 2017 case, CO2 data for rich countries lagged by years while GDP figures could be weeks old. One number arrives in a jacket; another is still on the road.

Foresight 2011 adds a third warning. The UK Government Office for Science found that many dramatic climate-migration estimates leaned on one or two original sources. Repetition made weak numbers sound settled. That does not make climate change small. It means a huge claim still needs its source route checked.

The route check has three parts. Name the path the risk uses. Ask how current the evidence is. Choose a step that can be corrected. The small step is not timid. It keeps the next fact close enough to change the plan.
breakdown.fullRead:
Ella reads two drafts of a migration brief and feels the trap tighten. One draft shouts a giant number and will wake people up. The other says Foresight 2011 found weak source chains and adaptation gaps, and it may sound less dramatic. The danger is real. The certainty is not.

Here is the hard edge. Factfulness does not say calm down and do nothing. It says do not let fear pick the method. A bad roadblock can waste staff. A stale CO2 figure can fake precision. A repeated migration estimate can turn a thin source into public truth.

Climate change belongs in the serious-risk pile. So do global pandemic, financial collapse, world war, climate change and resource plunder, and extreme poverty. Those are the five global risks named in the source. Serious risk deserves clean facts, not louder fear.

Hunter sees this when one climate graphic updates before the emissions table. The map looks alive on the screen. It would be easy to speak as if emissions numbers were just as current. The useful sentence is plainer: this picture is fresh, and the CO2 table may not be. That sentence does not weaken the climate case. It protects it from a bad claim.

The same care helps with medicine. Antibiotic resistance is dangerous, but blanket panic can hurt people who still need cheap antibiotics to live. A rule that cuts overuse without seeing underaccess is not careful. It treats one danger as if it were the only danger.

Extreme poverty also needs this balance. Rates can fall while many remaining cases stay hard. Children, small-scale farmers, minorities, and people near conflict can still be trapped. A falling curve is not a permission slip to look away.

So the practice is disciplined speed. Move fast enough to reduce harm. Keep options open enough to learn. If a claim says there is no time for a check, give it the smallest useful check: route, freshness, side effect.

Blair can use the same test outside the news. A sales mailer says the price ends today. A manager says the team must pick one plan now. A relative sends a crisis link with all caps. Blair asks what would still be true tomorrow before answering. That tiny pause may save money, trust, or time.

There is a time to do the opposite. When the danger is direct and physical, do not hold a meeting with a pen in your hand. Brace the ladder before it tips. Cut the power to the sparking outlet. Wave the forklift to a stop. After the immediate harm is contained, bring the checks back. Urgency earns the wheel only when the road is short and visible.

examples.title: Yvonne's Cordon Map
examples.scenario: "More guards at the roadblock" is the loud request in the room, and a firm cordon looks like control. Yvonne, at the response map table, spreads the Kikwit 1995 map beside David L. Heymann's Nature 2014 note. Three colored pins are left: one for the roadblock, one for Kwilu River dugout canoes, one for forest paths. The map asks for contact tracing where people can still slip past the cordon.
examples.whatToDo: Yvonne allocates the next planning hour by route, not by visibility. She keeps the roadblock in the plan but gives river and forest movement a named share of attention.
examples.whyItMatters: The planning choice makes urgency answer a practical question: where can transmission still travel? A response can be fast and still miss the path that matters.

examples.title: Ella's Migration Draft
examples.scenario: Ella, a Foresight analyst, stands outside the policy call with two marked drafts in her folder. One opens with a dramatic 150 million climate-migration number and will get attention. The other names Foresight 2011, the 10 million estimate, the 150 million estimate, and thin source chains. She must choose which page goes first: alarm that may drift, or precision that may lose the room.
examples.whatToDo: Ella keeps the risk on the first page but moves the big estimate below the source note. She says the warning is serious and the number is less settled than it sounds.
examples.whyItMatters: The choice protects both urgency and honesty. A reader learns that cutting overconfidence is not the same as cutting concern.

examples.title: Blair and Bailey's Data Lag
examples.scenario: "This climate image looks fresh," Blair says on the research call. Bailey answers, "The OECD CO2 table may not be." Blair scrolls to the OECD December 2017 note. "GDP figures weeks old, CO2 two years behind," Bailey says. Blair leaves the sentence unfinished and rewrites the caption.
examples.whatToDo: Blair separates the fresh image from the older emissions table. He names the lag in the caption before making a climate claim.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps precision from leaking across data streams. A fresh picture can support action without pretending every number is equally current.

examples.title: Hunter's Freshness Reveal
examples.scenario: The climate packet opens with a fresh-looking image, and Hunter expects the rest of the numbers to move at the same pace. The reveal sits in the OECD December 2017 note: GDP figures weeks old, CO2 two years behind in the cited case.
examples.whatToDo: Hunter marks each chart with its own date before drafting the urgent summary. He treats freshness as a property of the indicator, not the topic.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal breaks a common shortcut. A topic can be urgent while some of its best official numbers still arrive slowly.

examples.title: Finn's Source Thread
examples.scenario:
Junior analyst Finn folds the migration panel program into his coat pocket and finds a seat on the train.
Finn: This 150 million migration number is everywhere.
Donovan: Foresight 2011 asks where it came from.
Finn: Same issue with the 10 million estimate?
Donovan: Often one or two sources. Check UNHCR migration statistics too.
Finn: So not fake?
Donovan: Serious risk. Softer certainty.
examples.whatToDo: Finn keeps the climate-migration warning but adds a source-chain line before sharing the figure. He does not let repetition count as verification.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows how to slow one number without dismissing the people at risk. Repeated estimates still need a first-source check.

examples.title: Donovan's All-Caps Reset
examples.scenario: Three checks stand between Donovan and the send button: route, freshness, side effect. His routine is to forward the crisis link before the phone call ends. The message uses all caps and says there is no time. His thumb is already over send. He stops, places the phone on the coffee table, and restarts aloud through the three. The caller waits while he checks the first source.
examples.whatToDo: Donovan breaks the forward-first habit by moving the phone out of his hand. He names the route, the data age, and one possible side effect before responding.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is not delay for its own sake. It turns urgent energy into a smaller action that can still learn.

questions.prompt: Yvonne sees a strict Ebola roadblock on the main road, but the contact map shows river and forest movement. Which reading fits the urgency rule?
choices: The roadblock should be judged by how visible and orderly it looks to worried people.
The roadblock should be tested against routes contacts can still use to move.
The roadblock should be replaced by a slower review before any field action starts.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says controls can fail when contacts move by canoe or forest path. Visibility is not enough, and the answer is not slow review; it is checking the route.

questions.prompt: Ella hears a policy call turn into two options: publish the scariest number or ignore the issue. What should she challenge?
choices: She should challenge the either-or frame and keep room for ranges, checks, and options.
She should challenge the slowest speaker and push the group toward a single public line.
She should challenge the topic itself until the group can prove there is no uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 warns that urgency creates false binaries. Ella should keep ranges and options alive, not force one line or treat uncertainty as denial.

questions.prompt: Hunter is writing a public caption for a fresh-looking climate image and an older OECD emissions table. The packet looks current. Which check comes first?
choices: He should treat the official tables as current because the climate image updated today.
He should delay the whole packet until every indicator can share one reporting date.
He should mark each indicator's own publication lag before claiming precision.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says data freshness differs by indicator. GDP and CO2 can have very different lags, so Hunter needs dates per measure, not one shared clock.

questions.prompt: Finn sees the same climate-migration estimate quoted in many reports. What is the first inference Foresight 2011 supports?
choices: The repeated number has become reliable enough because many writers now cite it.
The repeated number may still trace back to a thin chain of original sources.
The repeated number should be ignored until migration stops changing across regions.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says repetition can amplify weak original estimates. The issue is source-chain strength, not the number's fame or a reason to ignore migration.

questions.prompt: Bailey is editing a climate handout and removes one single apocalypse story. A colleague says that sounds like denial. Which response best fits the evidence?
choices: He should accept the single story because severe risks need one clear public scenario.
He should narrow the climate topic because complex causes make public action less clear.
He should say climate is severe even when no one scenario explains the whole future.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 separates serious climate risk from one simple event. Rejecting a single catastrophe frame is not denial; it protects a complex risk from a bad story.

questions.prompt: Blair is sorting risks for a public talk and moves pandemics below daily worries because he thinks factfulness means less alarm. How should the risk list correct him?
choices: Pandemic risk belongs on the short list with financial collapse, world war, climate-resource risk, and extreme poverty.
Pandemic risk belongs below daily worries because broad progress makes rare events less useful to study.
Pandemic risk belongs outside the method because outbreak fear can distort every other fact check.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 places global pandemic on the short risk list. Factfulness narrows attention to major risks; it does not erase pandemic concern.

questions.prompt: Donovan hears a call to restrict antibiotics everywhere as the safest response. Which answer best fits disciplined speed?
choices: He should back the broad restriction because overuse is the only antibiotic danger in view.
He should ask for a plan that cuts overuse while keeping cheap lifesaving access where needed.
He should avoid the issue because resistance and access point in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says overuse is dangerous, but underaccess can also kill. Careful action must see both harms instead of turning panic into a blanket rule.

questions.prompt: Ella sees a falling extreme-poverty rate and wants to move the issue off the urgent list. What should she notice?
choices: The remaining cases can be harder because many people are children, small-scale farmers, minorities, or near conflict.
The falling rate proves the remaining cases will keep falling if no one changes the current plan.
The rate matters less than the headline because urgency should focus on whatever scares people most.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says extreme poverty remains an ongoing risk. A falling rate does not erase the harder remaining cases or justify headline-driven attention.

questions.prompt: A crisis link arrives while Finn is in a group chat, and the sender says delay is dangerous. Which response uses disciplined speed?
choices: He should share first, then check later, because urgent action loses value if verification slows it.
He should wait for a perfect report, because small checks cannot protect people from urgent claims.
He should take one small step that checks the route, freshness, or side effect before he spreads it.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 supports disciplined speed: small checks keep facts in the loop. It rejects both blind sharing and waiting for perfect certainty.

reviewCards.front: How does the urgency instinct change a hard problem in your mind?
reviewCards.back: It makes a complex risk feel like a now-or-never choice. That pressure can stop data checks, hide side effects, and make visible action look better than aimed action.

reviewCards.front: Why did the Ebola roadblock warning matter in Kikwit 1995?
reviewCards.back: David L. Heymann's warning showed that a cordon can look forceful while contacts move through other routes, such as Kwilu River dugout canoes or forest paths.

reviewCards.front: What does the OECD lag case teach about fresh-looking data?
reviewCards.back: A climate image can look current while related official figures lag. The OECD December 2017 example pairs GDP figures weeks old, CO2 two years behind.

reviewCards.front: What should you check when a climate-migration number appears everywhere?
reviewCards.back: Check the first source chain and the adaptation assumptions. Dramatic climate-migration estimates can rest on thin source chains.

reviewCards.front: What are the three checks in Check the Urgent Route?
reviewCards.back: Name the path the risk uses, ask how current the evidence is, and choose a small step that can be corrected after the next fact arrives.

reviewCards.front: What does the generalization instinct (Ch 6) get WRONG if you applied it naively to the Ebola roadblocks case?
reviewCards.back: It might treat roadblocks as one category and assume the label predicts success. This case needs route checks: road, river, and forest paths behave differently.

implementationPlan.title: Check the Urgent Route
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning pressure into a route check. Name the path the danger uses, the age of the evidence, and one side effect of your first response. The skill lets you move quickly without letting urgency erase thought.

ifThenPlans.context: When a visible fix feels like proof of action
ifThenPlans.plan: If the visible fix calms the room, then Check the Urgent Route by asking which path the risk can still use.

ifThenPlans.context: When a chart looks fresh because one part updated
ifThenPlans.plan: If one chart updates fast, then Check the Urgent Route by marking the date for each indicator before you cite it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a large number appears in many places
ifThenPlans.plan: If repetition makes a number feel settled, then Check the Urgent Route by tracing it to the first source you can find.

ifThenPlans.context: When pressure says there is no time to verify
ifThenPlans.plan: If urgency tells you to skip verification, then Check the Urgent Route by naming one small check you can do before the action spreads.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Urgency wants the wheel. The next claim that demands an instant reaction, jot route, freshness, and side effect first, then act on what they say.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of this week, look back once at the strongest urgent claim you met. Name what changed about your route check after you separated speed from panic.

memorableLines.text: Panic is speed without a steering wheel.
memorableLines.why: It gives the urgency warning a short image without praising delay.

memorableLines.text: A visible barrier can hide a leaky route.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the Ebola roadblock case into a useful test.

memorableLines.text: Serious risk deserves clean facts, not louder fear.
memorableLines.why: It captures the hard edge: concern and discipline belong together.

chapters.title: Factfulness in Practice
chapters.hook: I used to chase wrong facts; one stale habit kept rebuilding them.
chapters.counterintuition: The paradox is blunt: better facts can spread and old views can survive, because tools matter only when people build a habit around them.
chapters.tryThisNow: When you draft your next factual reply, ask one person, "Which fact am I treating as settled here?" Listen, then count the stale assumptions you defend.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Factfulness becomes useful when a person turns better data into a repeatable habit: ask one live question, count what appears, and update before the old story hardens.

breakdown.fastRead:
In a teacher chat for Gapminder Teach, Allison has a free lesson open and 3 wrong student guesses circled in red. The easy plan is to correct the answers and move on. The better plan is to rehearse the move: show the guess, compare it with the data, and ask why the old picture felt so true.

Factfulness in practice means building that move into daily life. It is not a badge for people who know more facts. It is a routine that catches a stale picture before it steers a lesson, a story, a strategy, or a reply. A habit beats a headline.

The rule is small enough to use: ask where the claim came from, count what you can see, then update one next action. If the routine is missing, even good data becomes a poster on the wall.
breakdown.deepRead:
The habit works because it makes error visible before pride protects it. A person can defend an old world map for years if nobody asks them to make a guess first. Gapminder Teach makes the guess public in a low-stakes way. A class can see that its first answer was not stupidity. It was an old picture that had never been checked.

Marc meets the same mechanism before a business plan is written. He starts with the old line: rich countries design, poorer countries make, and the West sells to the rest. Then he catches the mistake. Thomas L. Friedman 2005 helped people see services moving across borders. Fareed Zakaria 2008 pushed attention toward a post-American world. Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles make the shift concrete. Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya belong in the plan as markets and investment settings, not as charity backdrops.

That correction changes the next question. Marc no longer asks, "Where do we sell after the rich markets are full?" He asks which income levels are gaining skills, wages, and customers. Markets move when skills move.

The same pattern works for public facts. Tim Berners-Lee's linked-data vision makes checking less private. Gapminder bubble graphs let ordinary people inspect change instead of waiting for a gatekeeper to summarize it. Open data turns checking into citizenship.

The hard part is not admiring any one tool. It is choosing the next check while the old story still feels smooth. A teacher does it before a lesson. A business planner does it before a market bet. A reader can do it before sending a reply.
breakdown.fullRead:
Adele hears the worry before the training starts: if everything must be checked, nothing will get done. That fear is fair. Nobody can rebuild a worldview before every email. Factfulness in practice needs a small door, not a life-size research project.

The door is Ask, Count, Update. Ask one person a live question. Count one visible pattern. Update one sentence or one next step. The move is humble because it assumes the first answer may be wrong. It is practical because the work fits inside the moment before action.

Jacqueline and Nicole show the public version of the same habit. Jacqueline prepares a constructive journalism pitch by asking what context would make a bad event clearer. She still names the harm. She adds the base rate, the trend, or the local comparison that keeps fear from filling the empty space. Nicole prepares a local data display for Stockholm and starts from the reverse end. She asks what nearby fact people misread, then designs the picture so residents can test their own guess. One begins with a story that needs context. One begins with a place that needs a number. Both refuse the lazy choice between bad news and happy news.

This matters because local ignorance is still ignorance. A person can know the global child mortality trend and still misread the street outside the school. Alan Smith's statistics talk points to the same lesson: the facts nearest to us may be the ones we check least.

Business has its own trap. A map that says West and Rest feels tidy. Thomas L. Friedman and Fareed Zakaria helped crack that map open, but the new habit must keep going. Bangladesh and Cambodia do not stay frozen as low-cost production sites. Rising incomes can move textile work toward newer lower-cost regions such as Kenya. Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya can show up as commercial opportunities. The Atlas of Economic Complexity adds another check: look at existing skills and industries before guessing what a country can build next.

The open-data case adds the floor under all this. Public indicators, linked data, and Gapminder visuals make it harder for facts to stay locked inside expert rooms. They do not make every reader careful. They make care possible for more people.

The boundary is a person with a live duty and no room for a count. A paramedic treating a child at the curb needs hands free for care, not a worldview audit. The habit fits the planner, teacher, editor, analyst, and citizen before a claim travels. It belongs before the claim moves, not while someone needs hands-on care.

examples.title: Allison's Guess Board
examples.scenario: "The free teaching materials give the chart," Allison says, "but my students will still guess from the old world map. So start with the guess." Thierry taps the teacher community thread, unsure. "Won’t the wrong guess just stick?" Allison circles 3 likely wrong answers on the lesson sheet. "It stays visible and safe. That is where the practice begins."
examples.whatToDo: Allison writes the first student guess into the lesson plan before the data reveal. She lets the class compare its old picture with the Gapminder Teach chart.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange turns factfulness into practice instead of trivia. A wrong guess becomes material the class can inspect, not a private failure to hide.

examples.title: Marc's Map Correction
examples.scenario: Marc's first market slide says the West still designs while the rest makes and buys. Halfway through the caption, he stops. Thomas L. Friedman 2005 is in his notes, and Fareed Zakaria 2008 is beside it. Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles are not a footnote to the old map. Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya are not charity labels. Marc crosses out the arrow and writes, "track income levels."
examples.whatToDo: Marc corrects his own slide before the strategy session. He replaces a West-to-Rest arrow with a list of skills, wages, and consumer markets to check.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery matters because the error arrived in a polished sentence. The useful habit catches the stale map while there is still time to change the plan.

examples.title: Elaine's Linked Data Memo
examples.scenario: A source link blinks gray and dead under one chart, alive and blue under the next. Elaine catches the difference during pre-publication review and writes a saved draft message for the public explainer: "Before we publish, keep the source link beside every Gapminder bubble graph. Tim Berners-Lee TED 2009 is not decoration. If a reader can only trust our summary, we have made a prettier gate. If the reader can follow the public indicator, Gapminder bubble graphs become checks they can repeat."
examples.whatToDo: Elaine keeps the chart and the source path together in the draft. She treats public data access as part of the explanation, not an appendix.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo shows why open data is infrastructure for clear thinking. A reader who can inspect the source can correct the explainer too.

examples.title: Jacqueline and Nicole's Local Check
examples.scenario: Jacqueline opens her article draft with the frightening event and leaves a blank line for context: trend, base rate, local comparison. Nicole starts with the Stockholm visualization and asks which nearby number residents will guess wrong before reading. Jacqueline guards the story from panic. Nicole guards the map from smugness. Their plans differ, but both make the hidden assumption testable before publication.
examples.whatToDo: Jacqueline adds context before the story hardens into fear. Nicole asks for a prediction before the local data display gives the answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast keeps factfulness close to home. People can misread their own city as easily as they misread the world.

examples.title: Adele's Atlas Reframe
examples.scenario: "We can build any of these industries if the ambition is bold enough," the trainee says, finishing a grand list of future sectors on the development training call. Adele lets the claim stand, then points to the Atlas of Economic Complexity. "Ambition is not a map; existing skills are the trailhead." The trainee rereads the export mix and marks which capabilities are already nearby. The plan still reaches forward, but it stops pretending a country can leap from a slogan to an industry.
examples.whatToDo: Adele reframes the planning step around present capabilities. She asks the trainee to mark industries that grow from skills already visible in the data.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk makes diversification less like wishful ranking. A next industry is easier to study when the current skill base is on the table.

examples.title: Thierry's First Guess
examples.scenario: Thierry wants the first-guess column gone before the new teachers arrive at his onboarding worksheet, which holds two columns: first guess and checked answer. Allison has already written "keep it" in the margin beside the free teaching materials. The confusion is not a mess to clean up. It is the moment Gapminder Teach and the teacher community need: a visible old answer, a data check, and a safer way to change your mind.
examples.whatToDo: Thierry leaves the first-guess column on the worksheet. He plans the lesson so the learners see confusion before they see correction.
examples.whyItMatters: The school case protects the learning moment. If the wrong guess disappears, the class may get the answer without practicing the update.

questions.prompt: Two teachers prepare a Gapminder Teach lesson. Allison begins with student guesses; Thierry wants to reveal the chart first. Which plan fits the practice claim?
choices: Thierry should reveal the chart first so students meet the right answer cleanly.
Allison should use the guesses so students can practice correcting a misconception.
Thierry should assign the reading once so the worldview update happens privately.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 points to reusable Gapminder materials and a teacher community. The practice is repeated correction, not one clean reveal or one private reading.

questions.prompt: Marc's draft treats global business as rich countries selling to the rest. Which revision follows the Friedman and Zakaria source thread?
choices: He should keep the West-to-Rest frame but add more export examples from poorer regions.
He should focus on rich-country demand first and treat lower levels as future buyers.
He should track skills, wages, and consumers as industries move across income levels.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 says services and industries shift across income levels. The stale move is West selling to Rest, even when it adds more examples.

questions.prompt: A sourcing note lists Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles and assumes low-cost production will stay there. Which reading should change the plan?
choices: Those examples prove textile locations remain stable once a country builds the sector.
Those examples show that newer regions should wait until all rich markets are full.
Those examples show supply chains can move again as incomes and wages change.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says development changes supply chains. The error is treating a low-income production location as fixed after it appears on the map.

questions.prompt: A briefing shows Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya only in an aid section. Which edit best matches the business lens here?
choices: Move them into the market scan as serious commercial opportunities to study.
Keep them in the aid section but add a note that growth may arrive later.
Remove them from the briefing until the investment case is already settled.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 frames Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya as investment opportunities. The aid-only frame is the common error, not the business lens.

questions.prompt: A development team wants a new industry because it sounds bold. The Atlas of Economic Complexity points elsewhere. What should they read from it?
choices: They should study current industries and skills before choosing the next capability.
They should rank national ambition first and use the Atlas after the target is chosen.
They should pause diversification until the Atlas names one best-fitting industry.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says the Atlas maps existing industries and skills into plausible next capabilities. It guides choices; it does not bless ambition afterward.

questions.prompt: Jacqueline covers a bad local event and adds context about trend and scale. A reader says constructive journalism means happy news. Which reply fits?
choices: It means saving the hard facts for later so the public can handle the context first.
It means improving the information around bad events, not pretending they vanished.
It means replacing one frightening story with a positive story from the same city.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says constructive journalism improves information quality. The near miss is thinking context means ignoring or replacing bad events.

questions.prompt: Nicole's Stockholm display shows that several common local guesses are wrong. Which conclusion should she draw before launch?
choices: Local facts deserve the same correction habit as global facts.
Local facts are easier to know, so one clear display should end the issue.
Local facts matter less than global gaps because people live near them.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says local data can reveal local misconceptions. The error is assuming only global facts need correction or that nearness makes knowledge easy.

questions.prompt: Elaine updated a chart last month and now treats the worldview issue as solved. Which response fits the maintenance claim?
choices: She should archive the chart as proof that the team already learned the correction.
She should keep a routine for checking facts, sources, and categories again.
She should wait for a major error before reopening the team's assumptions.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says factfulness is maintenance. A corrected chart can go stale; waiting for a major error lets the old story rebuild.

questions.prompt: A teacher community shares one reusable misconception test and one lecture script. Which tool best fits the teaching point here?
choices: The lecture script fits best because it delivers the updated facts without a messy guess.
The lecture script fits best because a single clear explanation prevents repeated errors.
The misconception test fits best because learners practice seeing and correcting the old answer.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 supports reusable classroom materials, and the mechanism is practice with feedback. A lecture may inform, but it does not by itself rehearse correction.

reviewCards.front: What changes when factfulness becomes a practice instead of a slogan?
reviewCards.back: It moves from admiring better facts to using routines. A person asks where a claim came from, counts what appears, and updates a lesson, story, plan, or reply before the old picture hardens.

reviewCards.front: How does Gapminder Teach make misconceptions useful in a classroom?
reviewCards.back: Gapminder Teach gives free teaching materials and a teacher community for starting with visible guesses. Students compare those guesses with data, so they practice updating instead of only hearing a correction.

reviewCards.front: Why do Friedman and Zakaria matter for business geography here?
reviewCards.back: Thomas L. Friedman 2005 and Fareed Zakaria 2008 help break the old West-to-Rest map. Bangladesh and Cambodia textiles show why skills, wages, and consumers must be tracked as they move.

reviewCards.front: What does the Atlas of Economic Complexity add to a diversification plan?
reviewCards.back: It makes the team look at current industries and skills before naming the next bet. A country cannot build every bold idea at once; nearby capabilities make some moves more plausible.

reviewCards.front: Recall the fear instinct (Ch 4): in Jacqueline's draft, how does opening with the frightening event distort the reader's picture before context arrives?
reviewCards.back: Jacqueline's bad local event is the clearest moment. Constructive journalism adds trend, scale, or local comparison so one vivid story does not feel like the whole pattern.

reviewCards.front: Why does Tim Berners-Lee's linked-data idea fit the practice chapter?
reviewCards.back: Tim Berners-Lee TED 2009 points to checking as a public habit. When a reader can follow source paths behind Gapminder bubble graphs, the chart becomes something to inspect, not just trust.

implementationPlan.title: Ask, Count, Update
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching a stale assumption while it is still small. Ask one real person what fact you may be treating as settled, count the assumption you hear in your own reply, then update one sentence before it travels.

ifThenPlans.context: When a correction feels like it needs only one clear explanation
ifThenPlans.plan: If one explanation feels sufficient, then Ask, Count, Update by asking for a first guess and counting how many old answers appear.

ifThenPlans.context: When a market plan uses West and Rest as the map
ifThenPlans.plan: If the map splits rich sellers from poorer buyers, then Ask, Count, Update by counting which income levels now hold skills, wages, and customers.

ifThenPlans.context: When a bad story makes context sound like denial
ifThenPlans.plan: If context feels like softening the truth, then Ask, Count, Update by adding one trend or base rate beside the hard event.

ifThenPlans.context: When a fact check from last month feels permanently settled
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old correction feels done forever, then Ask, Count, Update by checking one source date before repeating the claim.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Listen to your own wording on your next reply about a fact, and count the stale assumptions hiding inside it. Tally them, then rewrite a single sentence to match what is true now.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, keep a running list of claims that lean on an old map, a single scary story, or a fixed country label. At the end, pick the pattern you saw most and rewrite one example of it in your own words.

memorableLines.why: It compresses the hard edge into one plain contrast.

memorableLines.text: Markets move when skills move.
memorableLines.why: It makes the business geography lesson portable.
